passage: The client's email arrived on Tuesday evening: the totals in Sachin's analysis did not match their own records. My stomach dropped. I had handed over the whole quarterly report with a two-line brief and a single check-in, on the last day. For a week afterwards I doubted every delegation I had ever made, and my hand hovered over the next task, ready to just do it myself. Then I reread my own brief. It was vague, and the deadline left no room to look at a draft. So I sat down with Sachin, owned my part, and split the next job into three pieces with a Wednesday check-in for each. It came back clean. I still feel a small flinch when I hand something over, and I am learning to let it sit there. Kashish

qa.q: What did the client notice in the analysis Sachin prepared?
qa.a: The totals in Sachin's analysis did not match the client's own records.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's hand hover over the next task, ready to do it alone?
qa.a: Kashish doubted delegating after the failure and was tempted to take the work back, which the hesitation shows.

qa.q: What would you advise Kashish to do when handing over a large task again?
qa.a: Split it into smaller pieces with regular check-ins, as Kashish did, so that problems show up early.

qa.q: How might Sachin have experienced the vague two-line brief?
qa.a: Sachin may have been unsure what was expected and had little chance for feedback, so the mistake was not only Sachin's.

grounding: The narrator doubts delegating after a junior's failure, reviews the brief, and delegates again in smaller steps with check-ins.

passage:
The auditors were due at nine the next morning, and at six in the evening Hemant discovered that the vendor files were a mess. Half the contracts were unsigned. Two suppliers weren't even registered. He had given the whole vendor onboarding to Manoj, his sharpest junior, a month ago.

Hemant's first thought was bitter: never again. I'll just do everything myself. He stayed till midnight fixing the worst of it, alone, angry, and quietly doubting himself. Was he just bad at trusting people?

On the drive home he replayed the day he'd handed it over. A five-minute chat in the corridor. "Take care of onboarding, you'll figure it out." No checklist. No check-ins. He hadn't even told Manoj the audit date.

The next week he sat with Manoj. "I set you up badly. Let's try again, smaller." He gave him only the registration step, with a checklist and a Friday review. Manoj got it right. The week after, Hemant gave him the contracts too.

qa.q: What did Hemant discover about the vendor files?
qa.a: Half the contracts were unsigned and two suppliers weren't even registered.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he stayed till midnight?
qa.a: Hemant felt bitter and angry, and quietly doubted his own ability to trust and delegate.

qa.q: What did Hemant change when he delegated again?
qa.a: He admitted his own unclear briefing, gave Manoj a smaller piece with a checklist and a Friday review, then added more once it went well.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen the task at the start?
qa.a: Manoj probably felt he had been given a big job with little guidance, not even knowing the audit date.

grounding: The story shows a manager whose junior failed a big delegated task, who reviews his own instructions and delegates again in smaller steps instead of taking everything back.

passage:
In the Jubilee Hills office of the event company, Avni stared at the photos from last night's wedding: orange marigolds everywhere, when the bride's family had asked for white. The family was furious. Avni had trusted Shreya, her new coordinator, with the entire décor order.

Avni felt let down, and then worse: foolish. Maybe she just couldn't hand things over.

Before saying anything to Shreya, she scrolled back through their chats. Her own instruction had been a two-minute voice note, recorded in a car, saying "the same flowers as the Reddy wedding." The Reddy wedding had been orange.

Avni closed her eyes. That was on her too.

She called Shreya in. "The flowers were wrong, and part of that is my unclear brief. From now on, every order gets a written sheet with colours and quantities, and you'll send me a photo of the sample before we confirm."

The next wedding, Shreya's sample photo came in two days early. The flowers were perfect.

qa.q: What colour marigolds had the bride's family asked for?
How did Avni feel after seeing the wedding photos?
qa.a: Avni felt let down and then foolish, doubting whether she could hand things over.

qa.q: What did Avni do before blaming Shreya, and why did it help?
qa.a: She checked her own instructions and found them unclear, so she could fix the process with written sheets and sample check-ins instead of taking the work back.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt when Avni admitted her brief was unclear?
qa.a: Shreya probably felt relieved and more trusted, not solely blamed for the mistake.

grounding: The passage shows a manager whose junior failed a big task, who reviews her own instructions, adds structure and check-ins, and delegates again instead of taking everything back.
